title: Retread memory: remanufacture retired server DRAM inside ECC shells
idea: Like tyre retreading, harvest DDR4/DDR5 from retired servers, re-test and re-bin at die or package level, and remount it on CXL expanders whose buffer chip adds strong symbol ECC, scrubbing and page retirement to absorb ageing errors.
why: Hyperscalers retire exabytes of DRAM every 4-6 years; recovering even 30% adds supply with near-zero new wafers, helium or EUV (scarcity, cost).

title: Row-as-codeword: in-DRAM LDPC turns overfetch into redundancy
idea: Po: the 128x overfetch is a gift. Each 8 Kb row is one LDPC codeword (~10% parity) decoded by a parallel bit-flipping decoder at the row buffer on every activation, fixing the ~80 raw errors per row at 1% BER; the same decoder writes corrected data back during refresh so errors never accumulate.
why: Makes 1%-BER cells usable at ~10% overhead (Shannon floor at p=0.01 is ~8%) with ~10-15 ns decode added to tRCD; overfetch (fact 8) becomes useful work.

title: Supercritical-CO2 decaffeination-style healing of capacitor dielectric vacancies
idea: Coffee is decaffeinated by supercritical CO2 that penetrates whole beans; use scCO2 carrying trace H2O2 or ozone, with no argon plasma or anneal ambient, to reach the bottom of 70:1 capacitor trenches at under 150C and refill oxygen vacancies in ZrO2/HfO2 that create the leakage tail.
why: Tightens the dielectric leakage tail (facts 1, 3) with a low-temperature, rare-gas-free step compatible with BEOL and 3D tiers; target 2-5x fewer tail cells.

title: Recompute-as-correction for KV caches and activations
idea: Ideal: memory errors are free to fix because the data can be regenerated. Closest: AI KV-cache and activation buffers are stored in unprotected relaxed-refresh DRAM with only a 16-bit CRC per 1 KB block; on a CRC miss the runtime recomputes that block from upstream tokens or layers instead of correcting it.
why: Facts 3 and 5: removes ECC storage and most refresh for the largest AI memory consumer; recompute costs <0.1% of FLOPs at 1e-7 block error rates.

title: Soviet scrapyard: transfer-print good tile dielets from defective DRAM wafers
idea: A Soviet engineer under embargo salvages everything: DRAM dies are laid out as mosaics of ~1 mm2 tiles, each with local periphery and scribe lanes; wafers with clustered defects are thinned and diced into tiles, and only known-good tiles are mass transfer-printed with elastomer stamps onto a roll-to-roll-made polyimide interposer with printed redistribution and a small CMOS controller.
why: A defect cluster kills a whole ~100 mm2 die but only a few 1 mm2 tiles, so good silicon from defect-limited lots is recovered (~10-25% yield gain on those lots).

title: Buckled-nanobeam bistable bit stores data mechanically
idea: A pre-compressed SiN/SiC nanobeam has two buckled states separated by an elastic barrier of ~1e-18 J (>1e5 kT), so it can't leak or relax. An electrostatic snap-through pulse writes it, a capacitive or piezoresistive gauge reads it non-destructively, and with no contact the elastic cycling exceeds 1e12.
why: Refresh-free, no charge tail, built on a U.S.-native MEMS process. Speed and density still need proof.

title: No counter SRAM: weak canary rows detect row hammer physically
idea: Imposed limit: zero bytes of activation-counter SRAM. Each subarray gets a few sentinel rows built with ~30% smaller storage nodes, so they flip after ~300 neighbor activations. They hold a known pattern, and a comparator checks them during normal refresh. A canary flip raises an alert that triggers targeted refresh of the neighbors.
why: Fact 9: ~1k-activation thresholds need MBs of counter SRAM per channel in counter-based defenses. Canaries cost ~0.1% area and track the same physics automatically as cells get weaker.

title: NICU-style first days: field burn-in under mirroring replaces burn-in ovens
idea: Neonatal ICUs watch newborns most closely in the first days, because that is when failures cluster. Ship DRAM without the multi-hour burn-in step. Server BIOS runs new DIMMs in standard memory-mirroring mode with aggressive patrol scrub for the first ~72 hours, retires any infant-mortality failures, then releases full capacity.
why: Burn-in ovens and test time are a real slice of DRAM back-end capital. Moving infant screening into the field cuts test capex and cycle time by ~10-20% (fact 4).

title: Endosymbiotic transfer: array dies keep no brains; logic die holds all
idea: Mitochondria moved most of their genes to the nucleus; strip memory dies to bare arrays with minimal drivers (no ECC, refresh logic, repair fuses or BIST) and hybrid-bond many of them to one logic-node 'nucleus' die that does sensing, strong LDPC decoding, refresh scheduling and fault mapping for all, so arrays use the cheapest array-only process.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die; moving it to a shared logic die and letting a strong decoder accept raw-BER-1e-3 arrays roughly doubles bit density and slashes process steps; with cheap array processes it targets ~100x.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pool lets capacitorless gain cells hold for hours
idea: Effect: carrier freeze-out and suppressed thermal generation at 77 K. A CXL-attached rack memory pool runs at 77 K, where generation current falls >1e10x and kT noise drops 4x, so 2-transistor gain cells with only ~0.05-0.1 fF parasitic node capacitance hold data seconds to hours and their tiny signals read cleanly. There is no capacitor module and almost no refresh.
why: 10x density: capacitorless 2T cells stacked 16 tiers give ~10x bits/mm^2. Same cost: no capacitor module or EUV; the cryocooler (~10 W/W at 77 K) is amortized because a refresh-free pool dissipates little.

title: Capacitively bootstrapped neighbor wordlines dip negative during activation
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: low-Vt planar | sense: standard | integration: monolithic with MIM coupling caps between adjacent wordline drivers | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. A small coupling capacitor between each wordline driver and its neighbours' hold nodes pulls neighbours ~0.5 V negative exactly while the aggressor is high, passively closing victim access devices; this lets a low-Vt access transistor run with a ~1.5 V wordline.
why: Constraint: no counter or mitigation-refresh energy (which grows toward several times access energy at hammer thresholds near 100), plus ~4x lower wordline CV^2, ~10x on the activation path.

title: Adesto CBRAM filament randomness pinned by single-nanopore 2D interlayers
idea: CBRAM (Adesto and others) stayed out of dense memory because metal filaments form at random sites, giving wide resistance spread and high-temperature retention loss. Fix: insert a monolayer hBN barrier with exactly one electron-beam or ion-milled nanopore per cell, so the filament always nucleates in the same ~2 nm spot and its neck is mechanically constrained.
why: Deterministic, zero-refresh resistive cell with tight distributions and better retention, enabling smaller margins and multi-level storage.

title: Bamboo septum: buried electron-sink implant between adjacent storage nodes
idea: Like bamboo's node walls that stop splits, a narrow grounded n+ sink implanted in the isolation between a buried wordline and the neighbor storage node collects electrons injected when the aggressor toggles, before they reach the victim.
why: Fact 9: attacks the charge-migration hammer mechanism directly; could raise flip thresholds from ~1k toward ~10k ACTs at <3% cell area.

title: Sense reference that slides with time since last refresh
idea: Worse: sense a cell that has decayed for 60 ms against the same fixed VDD/2 reference used for a freshly written one. Flip: each bank keeps a timestamp of its last refresh, and a DAC lowers the '1'-side reference along the measured decay curve, so sensing stays centered on the shrinking signal and the retention window stretches.
why: Fact 3: re-centering the decision threshold recovers ~30-50% of the margin lost to leakage, giving ~2x retention or ~30% smaller Cs.

title: Maskless per-die repair layer written after test
idea: Inverts 'every die gets identical masks': the one added litho step is maskless direct-write (e-beam or laser), personalized per die from its wafer-test map, writing a few hundred repair links that reroute weak rows and columns to spares far beyond fuse-bank capacity.
why: Repair is no longer capped by fuse area in the periphery (fact 7); a few % yield and much heavier weak-tail tolerance, with no physical mask to buy.

title: SPD-embedded factory retention maps standardized through JEDEC
idea: Combine wafer-level test data with the module SPD: a policy push for a JEDEC field carrying per-bank/per-row retention bins measured at test, so every controller can apply multi-rate refresh and weak-row placement from day one without slow in-field profiling.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): multi-rate refresh can cut refresh operations ~70% but needs maps; standardization unlocks it industry-wide at near-zero cost.

title: Row overfetch turned into row-wide LDPC in sense-amp stripe
idea: Reverse the 128x overfetch from waste into an asset: every ACT already senses a full 8 Kb row, so an XOR-tree LDPC check (~3% parity over the whole row) runs in the sense-amp stripe at activation, instead of SECDED per 64 b at the I/O. The row-wide code corrects 40+ bit errors per row, so cells with raw BER ~1e-4 (smaller Cs, longer refresh) become shippable.
why: Capacitor charge wall + refresh: tolerating 1e-4 raw BER allows ~30-40% smaller Cs or ~4x refresh interval; parity overhead falls from 12.5% to ~3%.

title: Magnify 3D tier count 30% and fuse off failed tiers
idea: Fabricate 3D DRAM with ~30% more tiers than the sold capacity, giving each tier its own select line and BIST. Tiers with low capacitor or transistor yield are fused off at test and in the field.
why: Fact 2: 3D becomes economic at ~90% per-tier yield instead of near-perfect yield, so the 26-tier break-even becomes a yield-tolerant target.

title: Eliminate uniform cell strength: significance-graded capacitors within each row
idea: Fabricate rows with two capacitor diameters (a column-mask variant, not an extra layer). About 1/4 of columns get full-size pillars for sign, exponent and high-order bits; 3/4 get thinner, shorter pillars for mantissa LSBs. The data layout packs numeric formats so each bit's significance lands on a matching column.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): weak columns can use a ~40:1 AR etch, raising yield and density ~20-30% for AI tensors, where LSB flips cost <0.1% accuracy.

title: Read-verify-only refresh for non-destructive gain cells
idea: With no capacitor, a 2T/3T gain cell stores the bit on the read transistor's gate and reads it non-destructively as current. Refresh becomes a cheap read scan against a 'decay-warning' threshold set above the decision level, and only the ~0.1-1% of cells crossing it are rewritten.
why: Refresh (fact 3): energy scales with decaying cells, not all cells, so 46 fJ/bit falls to a few fJ/bit and bandwidth is freed.

title: Band-offset Ge quantum wells store holes behind a heterobarrier
idea: Effect: heterojunction band offset. Charge is stored as holes in a buried SiGe/Ge quantum well under each access channel; the ~0.5 eV valence-band offset confines them so thermionic loss falls ~exp(-0.5 eV/kT), giving seconds of retention with no capacitor, and reads sense the threshold shift of the overlying channel (built-in gain-cell amplification).
why: 10x density: a capacitorless 1T cell at 4F^2 stacked 32 tiers by Si/SiGe superlattice epitaxy gives >10x. Same cost: the capacitor module and its EUV steps are removed.

title: No EUV: fat DUV cells drop on-die ECC and refresh
idea: Imposed limit: no EUV layers. Use relaxed-pitch DUV cells with ~2x capacitor volume and very low raw BER. On-die ECC (6.25%) is removed and the refresh interval stretched 4x, reclaiming area and bandwidth that partly offset the density loss.
why: Fact 4: removes 5-7 EUV layers from the bill. The reliability margin is spent to claw back ~10% of effective density and ~15% of bandwidth.

title: Zipper pairing: interlock weak and strong columns across chips per codeword
idea: Zipper teeth alternate: at module test each chip's retention-weak column groups are profiled and a per-DIMM permutation table in the RCD/buffer reroutes column bits so every ECC codeword pairs one chip's weak column only with other chips' strong columns, guaranteeing at most one weak bit per codeword.
why: A SEC code that dies at two weak bits now tolerates dies with ~10x the weak-cell density; marginal dies get binned into ECC DIMMs, ~5% more sellable bits.

title: Magnify charge only on weak rows via targeted overdrive writes
idea: Rows profiled as weak are written with boosted wordline and restore voltages (+10-15%) so they store as much charge as strong rows. The whole die then runs at the strong bin's refresh interval.
why: Fact 3: refresh is set by the retention tail, not the median. Lifting the worst ~0.1% of rows can double the die-wide refresh interval for a tiny write-energy cost.

title: One retention test only: per-row data whitening kills worst patterns
idea: Imposed limit: testers may screen retention with just one pattern. All data is XORed with a per-row keyed pseudo-random whitening sequence, so worst-case neighbor and bitline-coupling patterns become statistically rare. Refresh and test margins are then set for typical patterns rather than worst-case ones.
why: Cuts retention test time and the pattern-dependent guardband, recovering ~1.5-2x refresh interval and test cost per die.

title: Williams-tube read-around ratio revived as per-die fused hammer threshold
idea: Williams-tube memories lost to core, but had a working discipline: each tube's measured 'read-around ratio' set how many neighboring reads were allowed before regeneration. Fix today's worst-case row-hammer design the same way: test each die's real hammer threshold per bank, fuse it into a mode register, scale controller mitigation per bank, and price dies by threshold grade.
why: Stops sizing every die's mitigation for the worst die (~1k ACT, fact 9): typical dies run 3-10x less mitigation, and low-threshold dies are sold rather than scrapped.

title: Analog-computer droop compensation: time-aware sense references for hot memory
idea: Analog computers corrected sample-and-hold capacitors for their known droop by predicting the decay. The controller knows each row's age since restore from the refresh pointer (with a coarse per-subarray flag for recent writes) and reads the die temperature, then lowers the sense reference along the expected decay curve, so a cell that has lost 40% of its charge still reads correctly.
why: Water and retention (fact 3): memory runs at 105-110 C with standard refresh instead of 4x refresh, so facilities can use dry coolers instead of evaporative towers (>10x less water); ~2x retention margin at near-zero area.

title: Substitute supercapacitor hold-up with DRAM-process energy capacitors flushing dirty rows
idea: Keep a bounded dirty budget (e.g., 3% of rows) in a write-back policy and pair the DRAM with an on-die MRAM persistence tile; spare high-AR capacitor array area, filled with antiferroelectric ZrO2 energy-storage caps, powers the dirty-row flush on power fail.
why: Persistence at DRAM speed without NVDIMM supercaps/NAND: removes module BOM and makes HBM/DRAM persistent at ~3-5% area.

title: Series ferroelectric layer makes storage gate self-restoring
idea: Add a thin series ferroelectric to the gain cell's storage gate so the node's charge-voltage curve becomes S-shaped with two wells. Small leakage drifts are resisted until the coercive field, so the node stays latch-like. The bit remains charge-based, unlike a FeFET, which requires full polarization switching.
why: Capacitorless retention: aims for 100x rarer refresh and tolerance of leaky access devices.

title: QLC-flash logic for DRAM: half-height capacitors plus LDPC
idea: QLC NAND ships cells with raw BER around 10^-2 because LDPC corrects them. Build DRAM with capacitors at half the height (AR ~35, ~2.5 fF) and a raw BER near 10^-5, and put a 10-15%-overhead quasi-cyclic LDPC decoder, with a fast hard-decision first pass, in the HBM or CXL logic die so the external error rate meets spec.
why: Halving capacitor aspect ratio cuts the hardest etch and deposition steps and allows a tighter pitch (fact 1). Expect ~15-25% lower cost per bit after paying for parity and the decoder.

title: Tattoo map: weak-row map inked into on-die OTP, standardized in JEDEC
idea: The fab's retention and hammer test map is permanently burned into on-die antifuse OTP in a standard JEDEC 'weak map' register format, so any controller can read it and apply targeted refresh, ECC placement or remapping.
why: Fabs over-design because controllers are blind; a standard map lets them ship lower-Cs, higher-variability dies for ~10% density/yield gain.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM panel that maps out failing tiles
idea: Rule: defects are routed around, never scrapped. DRAM stays as an undiced wafer of tiles linked by a mesh network. Defective tiles are mapped out at test and in the field, and when enough tiles fail, the panel moves to a lower service tier rather than being discarded.
why: Eliminates die-level yield loss, dicing and packaging, and gives a gradual decline in capacity rather than a sudden end of life.

title: Genome-coverage redundancy: reclaim ECC lanes as data for self-protected pages
idea: Sequencers keep 30x-redundant reads, so single flips do not matter. On ECC DIMMs and HBM, the OS marks pages that are already protected end-to-end (erasure-coded objects, checksummed caches, FEC'd media, replicated weights), and the controller uses the 8 ECC bits per beat on those pages as data, exposing 12.5% more capacity.
why: Turns up to 12.5% of installed ECC capacity into usable bits on eligible pages. At fleet scale that is new supply without new wafers.

title: Clotting capsules: liquid-metal microcapsules self-heal cracked HBM bonds
idea: Seed the HBM underfill and bond interface with ~2 um gallium-alloy microcapsules; when thermal cycling cracks a microbump or hybrid-bond pad, the crack ruptures nearby capsules and the liquid metal wicks into the gap and re-closes the circuit like a platelet plug.
why: HBM TSV tax (yield down 20-30%, field opens): converts a share of stacking and cycling opens into self-repairs, raising stack yield and life and tolerating cheaper, less tightly controlled bonding.

title: Retrofit mature U.S. DUV fabs with one reliability mask
idea: Inverts 'competitive DRAM needs the newest EUV node': a policy-backed program funds mature 2x-nm DUV lines in the U.S. to add one RDL mask exposing every die's internal ECC syndromes and repair ports to a companion controller chiplet, which applies map-based tolerance so cheap, weaker legacy cells serve AI tiers.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4): depreciated, EUV-free tools add supply in ~2 years instead of 5.

title: Eliminate parity bits: flip-bounded number encodings for weights in cheap tiers
idea: Store weights in high-BER <=400 C memory using a number format built so that any single bit flip moves the value only a small, bounded amount: Gray-coded exponents, redundant thermometer-coded top bits and a saturating decode. No parity is needed.
why: Removes the 12.5% ECC overhead and decoder energy for weight storage, tolerating raw BER ~1e-4 with <0.5% accuracy loss.

title: Train models with bit-flip injection to tolerate 1e-4 BER
idea: Worse: train networks so fragile that one exponent flip derails inference. Flip: inject DRAM-realistic bit flips (directional, clustered by row) during training and use bounded activations and clipped exponents, so models run correctly from memory with raw BER up to 1e-4 and can be served from unprotected, refresh-relaxed DRAM.
why: Fact 3: inference memory can refresh 10x less often and weaker, cheaper cells qualify, cutting idle memory power 15-30% for inference fleets.

title: Wordline Joule pulses anneal retention traps in the field
idea: Reverse aging into healing: during maintenance windows a bank goes offline and high current is driven through segmented wordlines (far end shorted by a switch) to heat the local array to ~250-300 C for milliseconds, annealing the trap states behind variable-retention-time cells.
why: Retention tail / VRT: could cut tail cells ~2-5x and rejuvenate aged parts, allowing longer refresh intervals.

title: Satellite scrub-per-refresh: ECC engines inside every sense-amp stripe
idea: Satellites crossing the South Atlantic Anomaly scrub memory faster than upsets can accumulate. Put a small SEC-DED engine in each subarray's sense-amp stripe, so every refresh of a row reads, corrects and writes back corrected data instead of re-amplifying whatever is there. Single flips are cleared every 64 ms, so two independent errors never pile up in one codeword.
why: Double errors from accumulation are what force worst-case cell specs. Correcting at every refresh allows ~10x higher raw single-bit error rates for the same uncorrectable rate, which accepts weaker capacitors and leakier tails at a few percent extra periphery (facts 1, 3).

title: Exonuclease excision: per-row skip masks for 5%-defective cheap cells
idea: DNA polymerase proofreads each base and excises misincorporations; every write is read back, cells that fail are 'excised' by setting a bit in a short per-row skip mask kept in the row header, and the row's data is shifted past them on all later accesses, so a random point defect costs one cell, not a row or column.
why: Makes ultra-cheap high-defect processes (solution-processed oxide tiers, relaxed cleanroom, no laser repair) with 1-5% random dead cells usable at ~6-8% overhead, a prerequisite for ~100x cheaper media.

title: Racetrack shift errors fixed with disk-style servo markers and self-clocking codes
idea: IBM's racetrack memory stalled because domain walls pin or overshoot, so one bad shift offsets every following bit. Fix: borrow hard-disk servo practice by interleaving fixed marker domains and writing data in a run-length-limited self-clocking code, so the read head detects any over- or under-shift and re-shifts before decoding.
why: Turns catastrophic positional errors into ordinary correctable symbols, enabling capacitor-free magnetic shift memory with many bits per access device (density, fact 1).

title: ECC-tracked adaptive negative wordline off-level per bank
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: the fixed wordline-off voltage becomes a per-bank 4-bit DAC; when on-die ECC sees correctable retention errors rise (hot, aged or weak bank) it drives VNWL deeper (-0.2 to -0.5 V) to cut subthreshold leakage, then relaxes it to save pump energy and GIDL.
why: Leakage-tail suppression on demand: ~2-4x retention in the worst banks without a global worst-case setting; ~30% less refresh energy.

title: Tape AC-bias revival: dithered refresh pulses park VRT traps
idea: Magnetic tape needed a high-frequency AC bias to shake domains out of hysteresis and record linearly. Variable-retention-time cells toggle because one defect near the storage junction flips between configurations; a short high-frequency dither on the cell plate or wordline-low level during refresh, tuned to drive metastable traps into their low-leakage configuration, keeps VRT cells in the long-retention state most of the time.
why: Retention tail and VRT (fact 3): VRT defeats retention profiling and forces worst-case refresh; parking traps would let profiled multi-rate refresh work, giving ~2-4x longer average refresh intervals.

title: Dirty-silicon DRAM grown in non-Spruce-Pine crucibles
idea: Po: memory made from dirty sand. Wafers come from ingots grown in synthetic-silica or lower-purity quartz crucibles, accepting more oxygen and trace metals; the extra generation-recombination centers fatten the junction-leakage tail to ~1% retention failures, which the code tolerates.
why: Scarce resource (Spruce Pine >80% of high-purity quartz): removes a single-point chokepoint and trims wafer cost ~5-10%.

title: Leaky integrate-and-fire capacitor as per-row hammer sentinel
idea: Give each small row group an analog 'membrane' capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet per ACT and leaks with a time constant matched to the refresh window; when it crosses a comparator threshold it fires a targeted neighbour refresh and resets, replacing SRAM counter tables with one array-device capacitor plus comparator per group.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations: digital per-row counters cost ~1-4% die area and grow as thresholds fall; an LIF integrator gives continuously decaying counts that cannot be gamed by window resets, at ~10x less area.

title: Analog leaky-bucket capacitor physically caps row activations
idea: Inverts 'hammer defense needs digital counters': each wordline-driver group gets a small capacitor that every activation drains by a fixed packet while a resistor slowly refills it; below threshold the driver triggers neighbor refresh or refuses further ACTs until it recovers.
why: Row-hammer protection (fact 9) at ~1k-ACT thresholds without SRAM tracker tables, ~0.5% area versus multi-percent for trackers.

title: Wordline drivers with depletable charge budget physically throttle hammering
idea: Worse: let any row be activated as fast as the bus allows, so an attacker reaches 1k activations in microseconds. Flip: feed each local wordline driver from a small reservoir capacitor that refills through a high-resistance path; normal traffic never drains it, but repeated activations of one row deplete it below boost level, physically capping that row's activation rate under the flip threshold with no counters or SRAM tables.
why: Fact 9 row hammer: replaces counter-based mitigation (SRAM tables, stolen refresh slots) with a few-transistor analog rate limiter per driver and ~0 bandwidth tax.

title: Ant pheromone counter: analog leaky integrator tracks hammering per row
idea: Ants mark trails with pheromone that evaporates: each row gets one extra capacitor that a charge pump tops up by a fixed quantum per activation and that leaks with a designed 10-60 ms time constant; when its voltage crosses a comparator threshold, the neighbor rows are refreshed, so the hammer rate is measured physically with no SRAM counters.
why: Fact 9 row hammer: about one cell's worth of area per row instead of large counter tables, and it scales to 1k-activation thresholds.

title: TRR tracker overflow fixed with per-row analog hammer integrators
idea: Target Row Refresh died to TRRespass/Blacksmith because its few-entry aggressor table overflowed under many-sided patterns. Fix exactly that: each wordline driver gets a tiny leaky MIM capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet per ACT, a shared comparator fires a neighbor refresh when it crosses threshold, and the leak rate matches the refresh window, so there is no table to overflow or game.
why: Row hammer at ~1k ACT (fact 9): deterministic, pattern-independent protection for ~1-2% array area versus digital per-row counters and their tRC penalty; lets denser, more hammer-prone cells ship.

title: Replica-node relaxation oscillator times refresh from real leakage
idea: Effect: Arrhenius thermally activated generation current. Each subarray has a replica storage node built from the same cell transistor and capacitor that discharges to a comparator threshold, resets and repeats; its frequency tracks that subarray's actual leakage versus temperature, voltage and aging, and it clocks the refresh counter with a fixed guard factor instead of a fixed 64 ms timer.
why: Removes fixed worst-case temperature guard bands: at typical 45-60 C operation, refresh rate falls ~4-8x versus 85 C worst-case timing.

title: Kanban charge-bucket counters: analog leaky integrators per row group
idea: Kanban cards cap work in progress; give each row group a tiny capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet on every activation and leaks with a ~32 ms time constant, and a comparator fires neighbour refresh when the bucket crosses threshold, making an analog activation counter with built-in decay and no SRAM counter tables.
why: Per-row hammer counting costs counter bits and read-modify-write timing; analog buckets cost one capacitor and comparator per group and no bandwidth (fact 9) at under 1% area.

title: Leakage-clocked refresh: a diode array runs the refresh oscillator
idea: Ideal: refresh exactly as often as the physics demands, never more. Closest: a large reverse-biased diode array of the same junction type as the storage nodes discharges a timing capacitor that clocks the refresh counter, so the refresh rate follows temperature, process and aging automatically with plain 1990s analog parts.
why: Fact 3: removes the worst-case temperature guard band; ~2-4x fewer refreshes on average.

title: No digital state: leaky analog activation integrator per wordline driver
idea: Imposed limit: no digital counters or tables anywhere. Each wordline driver gets a tiny MOS capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet on every activation and leaks with a time constant matched to tREFW. When its voltage crosses a comparator threshold, the row latches a neighbor-refresh request that is served at the next RFM slot.
why: Fact 9: exact per-row hammer tracking at ~1k activations becomes ~2 transistors plus 1 capacitor per row driver, with no SRAM, CAM or controller state. It scales to any row count.

title: Refresh-as-migration: Feistel row remapping advanced by refresh copies
idea: Combine refresh with RowClone-style in-subarray copy: each refresh step copies one row into a spare slot and advances a keyed Feistel permutation of logical-to-physical rows, so physical neighbors of any logical row change every few milliseconds and hammering cannot stay on fixed victims; the copy replaces the plain refresh.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9): bounds per-victim disturbance without per-row counters, saving periphery SRAM/CAM area (fact 7).

title: Substitute contact-based NEMS switches with non-contact buckled-beam bistable cells
idea: Store bits as the up/down state of a nanoscale buckled beam held by mechanical bistability and toggled electrostatically, with no contact closure, so there is no stiction or contact wear.
why: NV with high endurance and no charge leakage tail; radiation-immune; avoids scarce materials.

title: Per-mat triple-well back-bias tuned to each mat's leakage mix
idea: Ideal: every mat sits at its own minimum-leakage point. Closest: put each mat in its own 1990s triple-well island with a small local charge pump, and set its substrate bias at test to balance subthreshold leakage (wants deeper bias) against junction and GIDL leakage (wants shallower bias) for that mat's measured tail.
why: Fact 3: per-mat optimization narrows the retention tail ~2-3x versus one chip-wide VBB.

title: S: sulfide threshold switch adds a leakage dead zone per cell
idea: Insert a GeS-based ovonic threshold switch (sulfur chalcogenide, As- and Se-free) between the access transistor and the capacitor; small leakage-driven voltage drops sit inside its hold-voltage dead zone and cannot drain the node, while full read/write pulses exceed threshold.
why: Decouples retention and disturb immunity from the access-transistor leakage tail (fact 3) and passing-gate disturb (fact 9); speculative but could remove most refresh.

title: Rotating per-epoch scramble keys break pattern-dependent failures
idea: No EUV: mature-node arrays show data-pattern-dependent retention and coupling failures. Time shift: re-scramble each row with a new key every few refresh epochs during scrubbing, so no worst-case pattern stays in place long enough to fail and errors become random and ECC-friendly.
why: Narrows the pattern-dependent tail ~2-3x, letting DUV cells with more coupling pass spec.

title: Minify ECC latency by speculating data and replaying on error
idea: Forward read data to the core before ECC finishes. The decoder runs in parallel, and on a rare error it raises a poison/replay signal that flushes dependent instructions, as after a branch mispredict.
why: Facts 1 and 8: long, powerful row-scale or soft decoders, needed for weak cells, add no common-case latency.

title: Checksum-carrying matrix math replaces ECC for AI weights
idea: Worse: insist every bit of weight memory is perfect before compute touches it. Flip: keep weights in HBM regions with no on-die ECC and relaxed refresh, and use algorithm-based fault tolerance (row/column checksums embedded in GEMM tiles) to detect corrupted tiles at compute time and reload them from a host copy.
why: On-die ECC costs ~6-12% area and adds refresh pressure; ABFT detection costs ~1-2% extra FLOPs while enabling ECC-free, relaxed-refresh HBM for read-mostly weights.

title: Silicon tunnel-diode keepers make cells immune to leakage
idea: Worse: let every storage node slowly bleed to ground so refresh is mandatory. Flip: attach a pair of series silicon interband tunnel diodes (degenerately doped Si only) to the storage node, forming a bistable Goto-pair latch whose negative differential resistance holds the node at either level with picoamp standby current.
why: Fact 3: removes refresh and the retention tail; an abundant-element alternative to SRAM at closer-to-DRAM density.

title: Anodised self-reforming capacitors like aluminium electrolytics
idea: Electrolytic capacitors heal oxide flaws by re-anodising under bias; grow the cell dielectric by wet anodisation of an electroless or N2-purged ALD Ta/Nb/Hf film (no argon sputtering or plasma), leaving a thin ion-supply layer so periodic in-field 'reforming' pulses re-oxidise new leakage spots.
why: A rare-gas-free dielectric route with a built-in self-healing loop against leakage-tail drift (fact 3); anodic Nb/Ta oxides at k~25-40 also raise Cs (fact 1).

title: VRT provocation pulses expose flickering cells in minutes
idea: TRIZ #9 Prior counteraction: during wafer test on U.S.-made memory ATE, short high-field gate/junction toggle pulses force variable-retention-time traps to switch states repeatedly, so VRT cells reveal themselves in minutes instead of multi-day retention soaks and are mapped out.
why: VRT is why refresh guardbands cannot be cut; reliable screening could allow 2-4x longer refresh and shortens test time, a key cost of a U.S. backend.

title: Doctor's vaccination: stress-test mirrored subarrays to find weak cells early
idea: A doctor vaccinates before the disease arrives: the DRAM rotates through its subarrays, mirroring one into a spare and challenging the original with lower array voltage, a 4x refresh interval and hammer patterns, so cells about to fail are found and the refresh bins and remap tables are updated before user data sees an error.
why: Retention and hammer tails drift with age; online challenge-profiling lets cells ship with ~10-20% less Cs guardband.

title: Zn: zinc sacrificial-anode rows absorb hammer flips beside hot rows
idea: Like zinc galvanizing steel, the OS page allocator and controller place only recomputable content (clean page-cache copies, parity, prefetch buffers) in rows physically adjacent to detected hot rows, so flips land where they are harmless and heal on re-fetch. Software plus firmware.
why: Turns row hammer (fact 9) from a correctness failure into a small cache-miss cost with no new hardware.

title: Speculative early data return with late strong ECC verdict
idea: Combine CPU branch speculation with ECC: the controller forwards raw data immediately while a strong multi-symbol decoder runs in parallel; on an error the core squashes dependent instructions like a mispredicted branch and replays with corrected data.
why: Makes heavy ECC (needed for weak or low-Cs cells, fact 1) latency-free on the common path, permitting 10-100x higher raw BER without adding 5-15 ns decode latency.

title: Minify sentinels: deliberately weak canary cells pace adaptive refresh
idea: Build a few canary cells per subarray with ~30% smaller capacitors or leakier access devices. A background engine checks them every few ms, and the refresh rate follows the first canary failures, tracking temperature and aging in real time instead of worst-case guardbands.
why: Fact 3: removes static guardbands, so typical-condition refresh drops 2-4x while staying safe.

title: Magnetosome chains: exchange-couple low-stability bits for collective retention
idea: Magnetotactic bacteria align magnetite crystals too small to be stable alone into a stable chain dipole; build fast spin cells with thermal stability ~20 kT arranged in short exchange-coupled chains whose collective stability is ~60 kT, writing by flipping one end and letting a domain wall propagate along the chain.
why: Refresh and retention tail: decouples write energy (single-cell barrier) from retention (chain barrier), ~3x lower write current than standard STT at equal retention, with no refresh and unlimited-class endurance.

title: Substitute unknown error positions with known erasures from weak-cell maps
idea: Store a compressed weak-cell location map (from wafer test plus online profiling) in a small fuse/NV block; the controller tells the decoder those bits are erasures, and an RS/BCH code corrects erasures at half the parity cost of unknown errors, so a die with 10x more weak cells ships with the same ECC overhead.
why: Retention tail and yield: raises usable dies per wafer and lets cells shrink capacitance ~20-30% (fact 1) since weak cells are tolerated at near-zero parity cost.

title: Eliminate unknown error locations: treat mapped weak cells as erasures
idea: Store the boot-profiled weak-cell positions for each codeword and pass them to the decoder as erasures. An RS code with 2r parity symbols corrects 2r erasures but only r unknown errors, so correction strength doubles at the same overhead.
why: Accepts 2x as many weak cells per codeword (retention tail, fact 3), or halves parity for ~6% more capacity.

title: Babbage's locking detents: time-to-latch flags ambiguous bits as erasures
idea: Babbage designed the Difference Engine to jam rather than pass a figure wheel resting between two digits. Each sense-amp group gets a tiny timer measuring latch resolution time (which grows as ln(1/dV)); slow-resolving bits are flagged as erasures and the ECC decodes with their positions known, which doubles what the same parity repairs (a SECDED code corrects 2-3 erasures).
why: Retention tail and sense margin (facts 1, 3): faded cells become located erasures instead of silent flips, so refresh can stretch ~2-4x or Cs shrink ~25% with unchanged ECC overhead; a few transistors per sense-amp group.

title: Known weak cells decoded as erasures, halving ECC parity
idea: Inverts 'errors are random and unknown': the weak-cell map from test and in-field scrub is held by the controller and fed to a Reed-Solomon decoder as erasure locations; RS corrects two erasures per unknown error, so the same parity tolerates twice the weak cells, or the same cells with half the parity.
why: Refresh can be set by the 1e-6 instead of the 1e-9 retention quantile (~4x longer interval), or ECC overhead drops from 12.5% to ~6%.

title: Leak-aligned inversion encoding keeps most cells discharged
idea: Po: memory that refuses to store ones. Retention errors only hit charged cells, so per 64-bit word the controller inverts the word (1 flag bit) whenever it would charge more than half the cells, respecting true-cell/anti-cell layout; sparse ML data then leaves only ~10-20% of cells charged.
why: Retention exposure (fact 3): halves or better the number of vulnerable cells, allowing ~1.5-2x longer refresh at ~1.5% overhead.

title: Li: lithium-6 rack neutron monitor drives space-weather scrubbing
idea: A 6Li-glass scintillator neutron counter per row of racks (no scarce He-3), plus public neutron-monitor feeds, lets the fleet raise scrub rates and ECC modes during solar particle events or at high-altitude sites and relax them otherwise.
why: Soft-error rate tracks neutron flux (~2x over the solar cycle, several x with altitude), so the fleet stops paying worst-case scrub energy all year.

title: Move retention screening out of the fab and into boot
idea: Po: the factory never tests retention. Vendors skip the long multi-temperature retention test on ATE and ship with mandatory on-die BIST that profiles retention during first boots and idle periods, burning a weak-row map into antifuses and retiring or refresh-boosting rows in the field.
why: Capital (fact 4): retention test is a large share of tester time and capex; ~30-50% less ATE time, ~3-5% cost per bit, and a faster ramp.

title: Magnify codeword spread across millimeters to defeat particle-defect clusters
idea: Display-fab particles kill clusters of cells tens of um across. Physically scatter each codeword's symbols across tiles millimeters apart, which is cheap on panels, so any cluster hits at most one symbol per codeword.
why: Hard cluster defects become correctable single-symbol errors, so panel yield follows random defect density rather than clustering and ECC stays light.

title: 77 K liquid-nitrogen memory racks permit 1 fF capacitors
idea: Scale+temperature jump (cell -> rack-level cryostat): at 77 K junction and GIDL leakage fall by orders of magnitude, so retention runs from hours to days. Size cells for ~1 fF (shallower, AR ~20:1 pillars) and operate whole LN2-cooled memory racks almost refresh-free.
why: Attacks the capacitor charge wall and the refresh tail together: capacitor etch depth drops ~3x and refresh energy almost vanishes; cooling overhead is amortized at rack scale.

title: Wordlines as on-die heaters that anneal retention traps
idea: Inverts 'a leaky cell is permanently leaky': during idle, a driver mode passes current end-to-end through segmented wordline metal to Joule-heat one mat to ~200-300 C for milliseconds, annealing the interface and bulk traps behind VRT and GIDL tail cells.
why: Periodic self-healing of the leakage tail (fact 3) could recover 2-4x retention on aged parts and may reset hammer-induced trap damage.

title: Field error telemetry tunes chlorine etch recipes back at the fab
idea: Reverse the information flow: modules stream anonymized per-row error and retention telemetry tagged with die IDs to the fab, where it trains recipe corrections for the less mature Cl2/HBr and O2 etches replacing fluorocarbon steps, closing the yield loop in weeks instead of quarters.
why: Speeds yield learning for a PFAS-free process ~2-3x, making the constraint economically survivable.

title: Frequency-hopping row remap with rotating secret keys
idea: Spread-spectrum radios hop channels on a secret sequence to defeat jammers. The FPGA controller applies a keyed small-Feistel permutation from logical to physical rows within each bank. It re-keys gradually, one row-pair swap per refresh interval, so an attacker never learns adjacency and aggressor ACTs spread over many victims.
why: Removes targeted hammering and raises the effective threshold about 10x (fact 9) with controller logic only.

title: Per-row leaky charge-bucket counts activations beside wordline driver
idea: Row hammer is a counting threshold (~1k ACTs). Each ACT dumps a fixed charge packet from the wordline driver onto a tiny per-row floating integrator, which leaks with a time constant equal to the refresh window. When its voltage crosses a comparator level, the neighbor rows are flagged for refresh. The result is an exact per-row analog counter instead of SRAM/CAM tables.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): per-row tracking for <1% area, which closes the sampling gaps that TRRespass-style patterns exploit.

title: Die passport: on-die ledger makes recycled DRAM cheap to re-bin
idea: Rule: every die must be recyclable without full re-test. Each die carries a few-kB OTP or MRAM ledger recording its retention map, measured hammer threshold, PPR repairs, temperature history and error counts. Refurbishers read the ledger in seconds to re-bin and re-sell the die.
why: Re-test cost (the main barrier to DRAM reuse) drops ~80%, making second-life dies economical and raising usable supply.

title: Latent TSV stubs let retired DDR dies become HBM stacks
idea: Rule: every die must have a higher-value second life. DDR dies are designed with TSV keep-out zones and buried, unrevealed TSV stubs. Retired dies are thinned, revealed and stacked into low-cost HBM-like stacks for second-life inference memory.
why: Fact 6: turns retired commodity bits into scarce stacked bandwidth without new wafers.

title: Halftone dithered weight storage spreads cell failures like printer dots
idea: Borrow halftone/error-diffusion printing: keep the sign and top bits of each AI weight in protected cells, but store the low-order magnitude as a thermometer (dot-density) code across 3 unprotected, refresh-relaxed cells, with error diffusion pushing each weight's rounding residual into its tile neighbours. A failed cell then moves a weight by one fine step that averages out across the tile, instead of flipping a binary bit.
why: Lets ~70% of weight-memory cells run at raw BER ~1e-3 with 4-8x longer refresh and no ECC parity (fact 3 refresh energy, ECC area); trades a little density on low-order bits for large refresh and ECC savings on inference memory.

title: Active negative-capacitance bitline cancels bitline load for 0.4 fF cells
idea: Effect: Miller feedback and negative impedance conversion. Each bitline pair gets a small cross-coupled negative-impedance converter, enabled only during charge sharing, that cancels ~85% of bitline capacitance; the transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cb) rises ~6x, so a 0.4 fF cell develops the same ~100 mV signal a 5 fF cell gives today.
why: 10x density: 0.4 fF planar caps enable a 4F^2 vertical-gate cell (1.5x) stacked 8 tiers at ~0.8x per tier (~10x). Same cost: the NIC replaces part of the sense amp, and the high-AR capacitor module is eliminated.

title: Minify thermal gradients on AlN ceramic substrates to shrink refresh guardband
idea: Build thin-film memory arrays on planarized AlN or diamond-coated ceramic substrates (170-1000+ W/mK) so the whole array stays within ~1-2C. Refresh is set by the hottest cell, so removing hotspots shrinks the thermal guardband.
why: Fact 3: each ~10C of guardband costs ~2x refresh; isothermal arrays cut refresh ~2x and let weaker cells pass.

title: Riveted hybrid bonds: redundant pads with nitrogen plasma activation
idea: Shipbuilders put several rivets in every joint so one failure is harmless; activate hybrid-bond surfaces with N2/O2 plasma (no argon) and give each critical vertical signal three parallel bond pads feeding a majority/OR receiver, so voids from the gentler activation never open a circuit.
why: Makes argon-free bonding yield-safe for HBM and 3D stacks (fact 6: 20-30% yield loss), turning single-pad voids into non-events.

title: Substitute fixed-rate ECC with time-since-write graded ECC for NV
idea: NV data is first stored with a light code; as a line stays unwritten (cold), a background engine re-encodes it with stronger codes because retention loss grows with time and unpowered periods; an orderly shutdown re-encodes all lines to the strongest tier.
why: Allows low-barrier, fast, low-energy NV cells (weak retention) with ECC overhead paid only on cold data; ~2x write-energy savings on hot data.

title: Map bf16 mantissa bits onto weaker pitch-walk bitlines
idea: Rearrange data significance onto process asymmetry: fluorine-free spacer patterning (non-PFAS resists, Cl/HBr/O2 etches) enlarges SAQP pitch walk so alternate bitline sets are systematically weaker; the controller maps sign/exponent bits onto strong lines and low mantissa bits onto weak lines without ECC.
why: AI tensors tolerate low-mantissa errors, so larger pitch-walk variation is accepted without yield loss or extra patterning precision.

title: Deep-space image downlinks: ECC bits spent only on high-order bits
idea: Space probes protect image headers and coarse coefficients far more heavily than fine detail. The host controller repurposes the standard 8 ECC bits per 64-bit beat into a double-error-correcting code over only the sign, exponent and high bits of BF16/INT8 values, leaving low bits unprotected. The DIMM or HBM still stores 72 bits per beat; only the encoder changes.
why: For AI data, low-bit errors are harmless, so concentrating parity roughly triples correction where it matters and tolerates ~10x higher raw BER (relaxed refresh, weak bins) at no capacity cost (fact 3).

title: Minify temperature: sealed -30C DIMM enclosures stretch retention 1000x
idea: Run DRAM in sealed, dry-nitrogen DIMM enclosures held near -30C by thermoelectric or two-phase cold plates, so condensation cannot form. Junction and GIDL leakage roughly halve per 10C, so retention rises ~1000x versus 85C operation.
why: Fact 3: refresh drops to once every tens of seconds and the 13 fA leakage-tail spec relaxes, so fabs can ship weaker access-transistor bins. In dense AI racks, cooling energy can cost less than the refresh and yield it saves.

title: HP memristor variability averaged by five-device vertical voting pillars
idea: HP's TaOx memristor program died on device-to-device variability and random forming. Fix: build five tiny switching layers in parallel along one vertical pillar so the sense amp reads their summed conductance; variability shrinks by ~sqrt(5) and one dead device costs margin, not data.
why: Tolerates ~30%-sigma devices without verify loops; in 3D the extra tiers are cheap, so density barely drops while yield rises sharply.

title: Substitute SRAM hammer counters with analog activation-integrating witness cells
idea: Replace per-row digital activation counters with one tiny floating-node 'witness' cell per row pair that gets a fixed charge packet pumped onto it each time a neighbor wordline fires (capacitive coupling pump); crossing a threshold flags a victim refresh, and normal refresh resets it.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9): removes the SRAM/CAM counter area and power from periphery (fact 7) while tracking every row exactly, not just sampled ones.

title: Painter's underlayer: MSB bit-planes in strong rows, LSB planes in weak
idea: A painter spends care on the underdrawing and lets the glaze be loose: the controller transposes numeric tensors into bit-planes, puts sign, exponent and high-order planes in ECC-protected rows on the normal refresh schedule, and puts low-order mantissa planes in tail-prone rows refreshed 8x less often and without ECC.
why: Fact 3: an estimated 30-40% refresh-energy cut on AI workloads, and tail rows are used rather than repaired or fused out.

title: KV-cache-grade rows: full cells for exponents, cheap cells for mantissas
idea: AI KV-caches and weights survive flipped low mantissa bits but not flipped exponents. Build a 'BF16-graded' region where hard-wired bit-lane routing places sign, exponent and high mantissa bits in standard ~5 fF cells on normal refresh. The 8 low mantissa bits go in half-height (AR ~35, ~2.5 fF) capacitors on a relaxed 256 ms refresh with no retention guarantee.
why: Half of the bits avoid the AR 60-75 capacitor and most refresh: ~20-30% less refresh energy and a cheaper capacitor module for AI memory, at <0.1% accuracy loss (facts 1, 3).

title: Masoretic letter counts as Berger tags catch every one-way decay
idea: Masoretic scribes verified scrolls by counting letters, which exposes any omission. DRAM retention loss is one-way (charged to discharged, per physical cell polarity), so each 64-bit word carries a 7-bit complemented count of physically charged cells (a Berger code): any number of leakage flips lowers the data count and raises the tag, so detection is guaranteed, and on mismatch the controller re-reads with a lowered reference to locate the faded cells.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): guaranteed detection of all leakage errors for 7 bits per 64 lets refresh be relaxed 2-4x safely with a repair fallback, roughly halving refresh's 16-33% share of idle power.

title: Eliminate hydrogen: hydrogen-free deposition plus titanium getters for oxide channels
idea: Hydrogen is a shallow donor in oxide semiconductors and the main source of their off-current tail and drift. Deposit the channel, gate dielectric and passivation below 350 C using hydrogen-free PVD/ALD (O3 or plasma O2, non-hydride precursors), and embed Ti/TiN getter islands that trap any residual H.
why: Tightens the leakage tail and drift of BEOL access devices, raising worst-case retention ~10x and shrinking ECC and refresh margins; no high-temperature anneal needed.

title: Drop array voltage to 0.6 V, buy margin with ECC
idea: Restore energy goes as CV^2, so the true optimum is minimum (restore + decode) energy, not zero raw errors. Run VARY at 0.6 V (2.8x less CV^2), accept raw BER ~1e-5 from the reduced signal, and correct with a 2-error code in the base die.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): ~2x lower array and refresh energy.

title: Battle-short mode: zero out uncorrectable AI weights and keep running
idea: A military 'battle short' bypasses protective trips during combat. In AI inference, when the controller reports a poisoned (uncorrectable) line from a weight region, the runtime substitutes zeros or the per-channel mean for those 32 FP16 values and keeps going instead of raising a machine check. It logs the address so the page can be reloaded later.
why: Neural nets tolerate dropout-like loss of a few weights. Removing the crash penalty lets weight memory run on cheaper dies at higher uncorrectable-error rates (facts 3, 6).

title: Eliminate litho-perfect decoders: stochastic address decoders calibrated after fab
idea: Pattern dense BEOL crossbar arrays with room-temperature nanoimprint, and build address decoders from randomly doped or randomly gated thin-film lines whose codes are unknown at fab. After fab, a discovery routine probes each line's response and stores a logical-to-physical code table.
why: Removes the overlay and litho precision the periphery demands (facts 4, 7) and turns random defects into table entries, enabling cheap, EUV-free sub-20 nm pitch arrays.

title: Mitsubishi cached DRAM revival: SRAM row cache absorbs hammering
idea: Mitsubishi's 1990s Cached DRAM and Ramtron's Enhanced DRAM put a small SRAM row cache on the die. Revive it as a hammer absorber: a 16-entry SRAM row cache per bank inserts a row on its second activation within a window, so repeat activations of hot rows are served from SRAM while the physical wordline stays closed, with an eviction counter that triggers neighbour restore if an attacker thrashes the cache.
why: Row hammer and activation energy (facts 8, 9): bounds physical ACTs per row below the ~1k flip threshold without per-row counters and cuts activation energy for hot rows ~90%; die area +2-3%.

title: Z-channel codes exploit leakage that only drains ones
idea: Effect: thermodynamic relaxation asymmetry, where leakage only moves a cell toward equilibrium. Data is mapped per subarray (true/anti-cell aware) so the charged state is always logical 1, making retention errors strictly 1->0; asymmetric-error codes (Varshamov-Tenengolts, Z-channel LDPC) then correct t errors with ~half the parity of symmetric codes, and write-side sparse coding (<=40% ones) shrinks the vulnerable population.
why: 10x density: ~100x more raw retention BER tolerated at the same ~8% parity lets poor-retention 0.3 fF thin-film cells stack 24 tiers (~10x) at the same cost.

title: Self-clearing aluminum electrodes isolate SrTiO3 capacitor breakdown spots
idea: Worse: build capacitors where one pinhole short kills the cell, and lean on Hf/Ru stacks to avoid it. Flip: borrow the metallized-film capacitor trick: a thin Al top electrode over a SrTiO3 (Sr, Ti, O) dielectric on TiN, so a local breakdown dumps current that oxidizes or vaporizes the Al around the spot, isolating it while the cell keeps ~99% of its area.
why: Fact 1: makes a very high-k (k~100+) but defect-prone abundant dielectric usable because breakdown is no longer fatal, meeting Cs at lower AR with no Hf, Ru or Ta.

title: Magnify light through glass: backside LEDs reset oxide-TFT threshold drift
idea: On a transparent glass substrate, a backside micro-LED/UV array illuminates idle tiles on a schedule to photo-detrap charge and reset bias-stress threshold shifts in the oxide access TFTs, followed by a mild thermal step. Dose and wavelength are tuned to avoid light-induced negative drift.
why: Self-healing: keeps the access-transistor Vt, and so the leakage tail, near day-one values for life, relaxing aging guardbands ~2x.

title: Battery reconditioning pulses that reset variable-retention-time traps
idea: Deep-cycle reconditioning breaks up sulfate crystals in lead-acid batteries. During idle, each row would get a brief reconditioning pulse: a deep negative wordline plus a raised bitline/substrate bias. The pulse empties the metastable gate- and junction-region traps that flip cells into their leaky VRT state. The pulsed rows are then re-profiled.
why: VRT is why per-cell retention profiling cannot be trusted, and therefore why 64 ms worst-case refresh is still needed (fact 3). Collapsing the VRT tail would make profile-based refresh safe, cutting refresh 2-4x.
